title: Nobody at the Pasar Malam Wants Your RM100 Note: Malaysia Market Money Myths, Corrected
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_markdown:
Ask a group of travelers how to pay at a Malaysian night market and you will get confident, contradictory answers. Bring lots of small ringgit. No wait, everyone uses Touch 'n Go now. Actually cards work everywhere, it's Malaysia, it's developed. Actually the auntie selling apam balik only takes exact change.


Most of this advice is either outdated or based on a half-understood glimpse of how Malaysians actually pay. So let's do this the honest way: take the most common beliefs about money at Malaysian street food stalls and markets, and correct them one at a time.


### Myth one: hawker stalls and night markets are strictly cash territory


This was true once. It is not true in 2026. Malaysia runs on a unified national QR standard called DuitNow QR, and the whole point of a unified standard is that one sticker works for everyone. That same square of laminated plastic is taped to the glass at a kopitiam in Ipoh, clipped to the umbrella pole of a satay cart on Jalan Alor, and mounted on a proper stand at a Pavilion KL boutique.


Watch the locals at any pasar malam. The person ahead of you buying lok lok is not counting coins. They scan, show the confirmation screen to the stallholder, and walk off with their skewers. The stallholder barely looks up. This is normal, everyday behavior from Kuala Lumpur to Kota Bharu, not a novelty for tech workers.


Cash still exists and still works, of course. But treating Malaysian markets as cash-only territory means you are solving a problem locals stopped having years ago.


### Myth two: those QR stickers mean you need a Touch 'n Go wallet


Here is where travelers get genuinely stuck. Many DuitNow QR stickers carry Touch 'n Go eWallet branding, because that is the wallet a lot of merchants signed up through. So visitors conclude they need the Touch 'n Go app, download it, and then hit a wall: the signup flow is built for residents, and foreigners frequently cannot complete it. We went deep on that exact frustration in[our Malaysia spending FAQ](https://moretapay.com/blog/malaysia-digital-nomad-spending-faq-duitnow-touch-n-go-2026-2026-09-08) , and the short version holds: you probably can't open one, and you don't need to.


The branding on the sticker is mostly irrelevant. DuitNow QR is interoperable by design, which means any app that speaks the DuitNow standard can pay that code, regardless of whose logo is printed on it. Moreta Pay is one of those apps. You top up a wallet from your own bank at home (a US account via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card), then scan the merchant's DuitNow QR like a local would. The app shows you the amount in ringgit, the FX rate, and the merchant's name before you confirm, and the stallholder gets paid instantly in their own currency.


So when the cendol uncle points at his QR stand, you are not locked out. You are one scan away from paying exactly the way his regulars do.


### Myth three: just use your credit card, Malaysia is card-friendly


Half true, and the half that's false is the half that matters at a market. Card acceptance in Malaysian cities is genuinely decent. Malls, chain restaurants, hotels, and mid-range cafes will take your Visa or Mastercard without drama.


But card terminals are expensive for small merchants, and QR payments are cheaper for them to accept. That economic reality shapes the street. The nasi lemak stall doing brisk breakfast trade has no reason to rent a card terminal when a free QR sticker does the job. So the places where you most want a payment option that isn't cash, the hawker centres, the wet markets, the roadside mamak stalls, are precisely the places where your card is useless.


Add the foreign transaction fees many home-country cards quietly layer on, and the card-first strategy looks even weaker. Scanning the merchant's own QR code, with the exchange rate shown transparently before you tap confirm, is both more widely accepted at street level and easier to reason about.


### Myth four: you should hit the airport ATM hard and carry a thick stack of ringgit


The classic arrival ritual: withdraw a fat stack at KLIA, then spend the next two weeks trying to break RM100 notes at stalls where a plate of char kway teow costs a fraction of that. Nobody at the pasar malam wants your big note. You will get sighs, you will get the slow counting of change from a biscuit tin, and occasionally you will get a polite refusal until you find something smaller.


The better play is a modest cash float, not a bankroll. Keep some small notes for the genuinely old-school corners of the economy: the pasar pagi vegetable seller who has done business the same way for forty years, a parking attendant, a stall where the QR sticker has peeled off in the humidity. Everything else, from the teh tarik to the durian stand to your Grab-adjacent snack runs, can go through a QR scan. Fewer ATM runs also means fewer ATM fees and less anxiety about walking around a crowded market with a wallet full of paper.


### Myth five: QR is a Kuala Lumpur thing, the rest of the country runs differently


Penang disagrees, loudly. The hawker courts around Gurney and the street stalls of George Town are dense with DuitNow QR codes. So are Malacca's Jonker Walk night market, Ipoh's kopitiams, and the Ramadan bazaars that pop up nationwide. Because DuitNow QR is a single national standard rather than a patchwork of competing systems, adoption spread fast beyond the capital. If a stall is set up to take digital payment anywhere in Malaysia, it is almost certainly taking it through that same standard.


This is a different situation from some neighboring countries where the digital economy thins out quickly outside the biggest city. If you are routing through Thailand on the same trip, the dynamics around PromptPay have their own quirks, which[we've untangled separately](https://moretapay.com/blog/thailand-street-food-markets-promptpay-money-myths-2026-2026-09-13) . In Malaysia, the honest summary is that the QR sticker travels further than your card does.


### Myth six: paying by QR as a foreigner will be awkward at the stall


The fear is a queue of hungry locals behind you while you fumble with an app and the stallholder loses patience. In practice, the interaction is shorter than a cash one. Scan the code, check that the merchant name matches the stall, enter or confirm the amount, show the success screen. No waiting for change, no mental math converting a crumpled note pile, no holding up the line while the boss digs for coins.


With Moreta Pay the flow is the same one Malaysians use, just funded from your home bank instead of a local account. And it extends beyond the street: the same wallet handles QR-based checkout on platforms like Shopee, Lazada, and Agoda, plus bill payments in supported countries, so a longer stay in Malaysia does not force you back into cash for the boring stuff.


### What actually belongs in your pocket on night market day


A phone with a QR-capable wallet, a small fold of ringgit in low denominations, and an appetite. That's the whole kit. The myths about Malaysia being cash-bound, card-friendly at street level, or locked behind a wallet you can't register for all dissolve the moment you watch one transaction happen at a real stall.
